case_study_insert.main_stem: Nova Vale Leather (NVL) is a private limited company in the leather goods retail and e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2011 by Sofia Vale, the business sells handmade bags and wallets through its flagship website, and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. NVL plans to invest $780,000 in a new eco-tannery and online fulfilment hub, financed by a $450,000 bank loan and $330,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $20.00 a unit and a selling price of $62.00, and currently produces 14,000 units a year. NVL faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 18% and finishing defects are rising as orders grow.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The workshop finished 3,400 leather goods last quarter at a defect rate of 3.3%, down from 5.0% a year ago. Leather offcut waste fell to 8% of material use from 12%. Staff turnover reached 18%, with 6 of 35 workers leaving in the quarter. Customer returns were 4.5% of orders. A survey of 400 online customers found 55% value handcrafted quality most, and 38% would pay a $15 premium for traceable leather. With 6 finishing vacancies, HR is comparing internal recruitment and external recruitment, and job rotation is being piloted to cut the 18% turnover.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Nova Vale Leather as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank increased the base rate from 3.5% to 4.25%, raising costs on NVL's $450,000 loan. (2) The national minimum wage rises 7.2% to $13.90 per hour from April 2026, affecting NVL's workforce of 35. (3) Raw hide and freight input costs rose 13.6% year-on-year, while consumer spending on luxury accessories fell 0.8% and online return rates in fashion average 17%.

questions.question_text: NVL is funding its $780,000 eco-tannery with a $450,000 bank loan and $330,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for NVL of using the bank loan rather than relying only on retained profit.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $450,000 bank loan lets NVL keep its $330,000 retained profit as a cash buffer against fixed costs of $210,000 a year and an 18% labour turnover that forces repeated hiring and retraining. Preserving that internal reserve is valuable when the eco-tannery may overrun and when customer returns already run at 4.5% of orders, so the business can meet short-term commitments without running out of cash.

Point 2: Borrowing the $450,000 allows the full $780,000 project to go ahead immediately, capturing the 38% of surveyed customers who would pay a $15 premium for traceable leather, rather than delaying until enough profit is accumulated. Faster completion lets NVL start earning from the new capacity sooner, and a predictable bank loan repayment plan is easier to budget for than an uncertain stream of future retained profit in a market where accessory spending fell 0.8%, rather than waiting for profits that may not appear if demand stays weak.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to NVL's costs, turnover, reserves and expansion.

questions.question_text: NVL wants to raise awareness of its handmade bags and wallets. Consider social media influencers, craft trade fairs, or search-engine advertising. Which should NVL choose to promote the range? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Social media influencers: Craft and fashion influencers can demonstrate the handmade quality that 55% of 400 surveyed customers value most, and can show the traceable leather story behind the $15 premium. Engagement is measurable and cost can be controlled. The limits are that results build slowly, depend on influencer credibility, and may attract followers who never buy a $62.00 leather bag, so reach does not guarantee sales.

Craft trade fairs: Fairs let customers touch and inspect the leather, which suits a product where handcrafted quality is the main buying factor, and they build personal relationships and word of mouth in NVL's niche. However, fairs are expensive in stand fees and staff time for a workforce of 35 with 18% turnover, reach only a small local audience, and cannot deliver the order volume needed to use the $780,000 eco-tannery.

Search-engine advertising: Paid search captures shoppers actively looking for leather bags, giving high intent and measurable return, and it can be scaled nationally to support the 14,000-unit output. The drawback is rising cost per click and strong competition from larger brands, which could consume the $42.00 contribution per unit without building long-term loyalty.

Recommendation: NVL should choose social media influencers as its main channel, supported by targeted search advertising. Influencers demonstrate the handcrafted, traceable story that 55% of buyers value and justify the $15 premium, something search cannot do and fairs cannot do at scale. Trade fairs are rejected as too narrow and costly for a business with 18% turnover; search is rejected as the lead channel because it wins clicks but does not build the brand story needed to sustain a premium price.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to NVL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of NVL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of NVL with a well-justified recommendation explaining why fairs and search-led are rejected.

questions.question_text: NVL's labour turnover has reached 18% and finishing defects are rising. Explain two benefits for NVL of using job rotation to improve motivation and reduce this turnover.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job rotation moves the 35 employees between cutting, stitching and finishing tasks, making work less repetitive and satisfying variety and esteem needs (Maslow and Herzberg). Greater job satisfaction should reduce the 18% turnover that saw 6 workers leave in the quarter, saving the recruitment and induction time that currently distracts the flat structure and protects the $62.00 selling price from disruption.

Point 2: Rotation broadens skills across the workshop, so cover exists when a finishing operator leaves and the 3.3% defect rate can be tackled by staff who understand several stages of production. Multiskilled workers help the new $780,000 eco-tannery and fulfilment hub run flexibly, raising labour productivity toward the 14,000-unit output target and reducing the 4.5% customer return rate caused by inconsistent finishing. Because NVL is flat with laissez-faire leadership, rotation also gives workers more autonomy, supporting motivation and easing the supervision burden on the 35-person team.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to NVL's turnover, defects and expansion.

questions.question_text: NVL has six finishing vacancies and 18% labour turnover. Consider internal recruitment or external recruitment to fill them. Which should NVL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Internal recruitment: Promoting existing workers into finishing roles is quick and cheap, and because they already know NVL's quality standards it should help reduce the 3.3% defect rate and the 4.5% return rate. It also motivates the workforce by offering promotion prospects, which supports job rotation and could cut the 18% turnover. The drawback is a smaller talent pool: with only 35 staff and 6 already leaving, internal moves create other gaps and bring no new specialist finishing skills for the eco-tannery.

External recruitment: Hiring experienced finishers from outside brings fresh skills and ideas, fills all six vacancies at once, and supplies the expertise needed for the $780,000 eco-tannery. It widens the pool beyond a depleted 35-person workforce. However, it costs more in advertising and selection, takes longer, and new staff need induction, which risks slowing output at a time when defects are rising; outsiders may also take time to match the handcrafted quality that 55% of customers value.

Decision: NVL should use internal recruitment for most of the six vacancies and external recruitment for one or two specialist finishing roles. Internal promotion is cheaper, faster and directly attacks 18% turnover, while a small number of external hires brings the new skills the eco-tannery needs. Wholly external recruitment is rejected as too costly and slow with only 35 staff; wholly internal recruitment is rejected because it would simply move the skills gap around rather than fill it. NVL should review the 3.3% defect rate and 4.5% return rate after six months to decide whether more external finishing specialists are needed.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of internal and external recruitment with limited application to NVL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of NVL.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, skills and turnover.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how NVL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $210,000 ÷ ($62.00 − $20.00) = $210,000 ÷ $42.00 = 5,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 5,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $62.00 − $20.00 = $42.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $42.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways NVL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 5,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 14,000 units to confirm the leather range is profitable, leaving a margin of safety of 9,000 units, which supports the $780,000 eco-tannery investment.
2. Use average total cost of $210,000 ÷ 14,000 units + $20.00 = $35.00 a unit to track the effect of the 8% leather offcut waste, setting a target to bring unit cost down as waste is reduced.
3. Use contribution per unit of $42.00 to evaluate the $15 premium sought by 38% of surveyed buyers: winning that premium on each of 14,000 units would add $210,000, so managers can judge the payoff from traceable leather marketing.
4. Use labour productivity of 14,000 units ÷ 35 staff = 400 units per worker to benchmark the new fulfilment hub, linking the 3.3% defect rate and 18% turnover to output per employee before further expansion.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 5,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $42.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 14,000-unit output; average total cost of $35.00 to track 8% waste; contribution analysis of the $15 premium; and labour productivity of 400 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate NVL's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has NVL's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.69 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.39 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.67 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $40,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $285,000; 2025 current assets = $185,000 + $65,000 + $55,000 = $305,000. The 2024 figure is $285,000 ÷ $190,000 = 1.50; the 2025 figure is $305,000 ÷ $180,000 = 1.69. Excluding stock, 2024 liquid assets are $40,000 + $35,000 = $75,000, giving $75,000 ÷ $190,000 = 0.39; 2025 liquid assets are $65,000 + $55,000 = $120,000, giving $120,000 ÷ $180,000 = 0.67.

Evaluation: Liquidity has clearly improved. The 1.50 to 1.69 rise means current assets cover short-term debts more comfortably, helped by current liabilities falling from $190,000 to $180,000 and cash rising from $35,000 to $55,000. The 0.39 to 0.67 improvement shows NVL is much less dependent on selling leather inventory to meet debts, important while it services a $450,000 loan and builds a $780,000 eco-tannery. However, the stock-excluding measure at 0.67 is still well below 1, so liquid assets do not cover liabilities, and trade receivables rose from $40,000 to $65,000, tying up cash at a time when 18% labour turnover and 4.5% returns already strain resources.

Conclusion: NVL's financial position has improved. Both measures rose, and the improvement is helped by inventories falling from $210,000 to $185,000, so it is not merely a stock build-up. The main residual risk is low liquid cover and rising receivables, so NVL should tighten credit control before committing further borrowing.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and cash movements and a justified conclusion on whether NVL's position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NVL of investing in the eco-tannery and promoting traceable leather.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The eco-tannery supports the 38% of 400 surveyed customers who would pay a $15 premium for traceable leather, letting NVL strengthen its $62.00 selling price and add to the $42.00 contribution per unit while differentiating from mass-market rivals. It also reinforces the handcrafted quality that 55% value most and helps justify the $780,000 investment, appealing to increasingly sustainability-conscious online shoppers.

Disadvantage: Building the eco-tannery needs $780,000 of capital and adds fixed costs beyond the $210,000 already incurred, raising the break-even output above 5,000 units and increasing risk if accessory spending fell 0.8%. Traceable leather may also cost more than standard hides, lifting the $20.00 variable cost, and the insert gives no figure for that premium, so the benefit of the $15 charge cannot be confirmed; if customers reject it, margins will suffer while 18% turnover and 3.3% defects persist. With accessory spending already down 0.8%, NVL cannot assume buyers will accept a higher price.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to NVL's survey, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise from 3.5% to 4.25%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 13.6% rise in raw hide and freight costs will affect NVL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.5% to 4.25%): If NVL's $450,000 loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is significant next to fixed costs of $210,000 a year, and it would also raise the cost of financing the remaining $780,000 eco-tannery. If the loan is fixed, the immediate effect is zero, so NVL can reduce this risk by fixing the rate, and the fall in accessory spending of 0.8% is a separate demand concern.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, to $13.90 per hour): With a workforce of 35 and 18% labour turnover, this rise feeds directly into wage costs for cutting, finishing and fulfilment and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented. The correct benchmark is the given productivity figure: 14,000 units ÷ 35 staff = 400 units per worker. If productivity holds at 400 units and turnover falls, the rise is absorbable; otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $42.00 contribution per unit is squeezed.

Raw hide and freight inflation (13.6%): The insert does not decompose the $20.00 variable cost, so only a bound can be shown: if the whole variable cost rose 13.6%, that adds 13.6% × $20.00 = $2.72 per unit, or about $38,080 a year at 14,000 units. Even a partial increase would erode the contribution that funds the $780,000 project, and with spending on luxury accessories down 0.8% and fashion returns averaging 17%, NVL has limited scope to raise the $62.00 price.

Conclusion: The 13.6% rise in hide and freight costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every unit, is larger than the $3,375 interest increment and the absorbable wage rise, and directly attacks the $42.00 contribution on which the $780,000 expansion depends. The interest rise is smaller and manageable by fixing the rate; the wage rise can be offset by 400-unit productivity, so input inflation is the dominant threat.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to NVL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on NVL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of NVL with a well-justified judgment on which has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
